title: Planning: graphic organizers and prewriting
subject: LANGUAGE
subtopic: Plan, Organize; Create Cohesion, Use Transitions

slides.title: Plan first
slides.text:
Good writers **plan** before they write.

A plan helps you remember your ideas and put them in order.

slides.title: Two easy plans
slides.text:
**Web:** Write your topic in a circle. Draw lines to small circles with details. Good for **describing**.

**Steps chart:** Boxes with arrows: 1 → 2 → 3. Good for **how to do** something or **what happened**.

slides.title: Pick the plan
slides.text:
1. Read the writing task.
2. Ask: **Am I describing, or telling steps?**
3. Describing → web. Steps → steps chart.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
The task tells you which plan to use.

1. Read the task.
2. Find the clue words: **describe**, **tell how**, **first**, **steps**.
3. Pick the plan that matches.

sentences.t: The word describe is a clue.
A web lets you add many details around the animal.

example.explain:
The task says **describe**. A web holds many details about one thing.

So the web is the best plan.

together.passage: Sara must write how to make a sandwich. First, she gets the bread. Next, she adds cheese and tomato. Last, she cuts it in half. She likes cheese the most.
options: A steps chart with boxes and arrows
A drawing of a sandwich shop
together.hint: Is Sara describing one thing, or telling steps in order?
together.good: Yes! She is telling steps in order, so a steps chart fits.

sentences: Sara must write how to make a sandwich.
First, she gets the bread.
Next, she adds cheese and tomato.
Last, she cuts it in half.
She likes cheese the most.
evidence.stem: The answer was: a steps chart. Tap 2 sentences that show the steps.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells what she likes. Find the sentences with step words.

options: A web with details about the school
A shopping list for the week
checks.why: Describing one thing with many details fits a web.

checks.passage: Task: Tell how you plant a seed.
options: A steps chart: dig, plant, water
checks.why: Planting is done in steps, so a steps chart fits.

checks.passage: Task: Tell what you did on your last holiday, from start to end.
options: A steps chart: first, next, last
checks.why: Events from start to end go in order, so a steps chart fits.

again.title: Circle or arrows?
again.text:
**Circle web** = many details about **one thing**.

**Arrows** = things that happen **in order**.
again.example:
"Describe a camel" → **web**.

"How to wash a car" → **arrows**.

slides.title: Graphic organizers
slides.text:
A **graphic organizer** is a drawing that helps you plan. It shows your ideas and how they connect.

Different tasks need different organizers.

slides.title: Four common organizers
slides.text:
1. **Web:** a topic in the middle and details around it (describing).
2. **Sequence chart:** boxes in order (steps, events).
3. **Venn diagram:** two circles that overlap (comparing two things).
4. **T-chart:** two columns (for and against, facts and opinions).

slides.title: From organizer to paragraph
slides.text:
Each part of the organizer becomes part of your writing.

In a web, the centre becomes your **topic sentence**, and each outer circle becomes a **detail sentence**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
The writing task gives the **clues**.

1. Find the key words: describe, compare, steps, pros and cons.
2. Match them to an organizer.
3. Check: will this organizer hold the kind of ideas the task needs?

sentences.t: Task: Compare a cat and a dog as pets.
A cat can stay alone; a dog needs walks.
A Venn diagram shows what is the same in the middle and what is different on the sides.

example.explain: The key word is **compare**. A **Venn diagram** has room for what is the same (middle) and what is different (sides). That makes it the best organizer.

together.passage: Faisal's teacher asked the class to write about whether students should wear uniforms. Faisal wants to list the good points of uniforms on one side. He also wants to list the bad points on the other side. After that, he will decide what he thinks. His uniform is blue.
together.stem: Which graphic organizer would help Faisal most?
together.hint: What does Faisal want to do with his ideas? Look for the clue about two sides.
together.good: Yes! A T-chart has two columns: good points on one side, bad points on the other.

sentences: Faisal's teacher asked the class to write about whether students should wear uniforms.
Faisal wants to list the good points of uniforms on one side.
He also wants to list the bad points on the other side.
After that, he will decide what he thinks.
His uniform is blue.
evidence.stem: The answer was: a T-chart. Tap the 2 sentences that show he needs two columns.
evidence.wrong: This sentence gives the task, his next step, or his uniform colour. Find the sentences about the two lists.

checks.passage: Task: Describe the city of Abha for a travel poster.
options: A T-chart of good and bad points
A Venn diagram of two cities
A web with Abha in the centre
checks.why: Describing one place with many details fits a web.

checks.passage: Task: Compare summer and winter in your city.
checks.why: A Venn diagram shows how the two seasons are alike and different.

checks.passage: Task: Explain how to make a paper plane, step by step.
checks.why: Steps in order fit a sequence chart.

again.title: Match the key word
again.text:
**Describe** → web
**Steps / events** → sequence chart
**Compare** → Venn diagram
**Two sides** → T-chart
again.example: "Write about the pros and cons of video games" → **two sides** → **T-chart**.

slides.title: The right tool for the job
slides.text:
Choosing the **most appropriate** organizer saves time and makes writing clearer.

The wrong organizer can hide important connections, like causes and effects or the order of events.

slides.title: More organizers
slides.text:
1. **Cause-and-effect chart:** shows what happened and why.
2. **Timeline:** shows events by date.
3. **Main idea and details chart:** one big idea with supporting facts.
4. **Problem-and-solution chart:** a problem, then possible solutions.

slides.title: Build up your topic
slides.text:
An organizer also helps you **develop** a topic: you can see which parts have many details and which need more.

If one box is empty, that is where you need to do more thinking or research.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To choose the best organizer, find the **purpose** of the writing.

1. Look for clue words: because, as a result (cause and effect); in 1950, later (timeline); problem, fix (problem and solution).
2. Find the sentences that show what the writer must explain.
3. Choose the organizer that shows **that** kind of connection.

sentences.t: Topic: The history of the Hejaz Railway.
It carried pilgrims to Madinah for several years.
Clue: dates and events in order point to a timeline.

example.explain: The topic is history, and the facts come with **dates**. A **timeline** shows each event in its place in time. It is the best organizer for this report.

together.passage: Huda is writing a report on why the school's plants died last summer. She found that the gardener was away for two weeks, so nobody watered the plants. She also learned that the hot sun burned the leaves because there was no shade. Her report must show each reason and what it caused. She will add photos at the end.
together.stem: Which graphic organizer is most appropriate for Huda's report?
options: A timeline of the school's history
together.hint: What does Huda need to show? Look for words like "so" and "because".
together.good: Yes! Her report shows causes (no water, no shade) and their effects, so a cause-and-effect chart fits.

sentences: Huda is writing a report on why the school's plants died last summer.
She found that the gardener was away for two weeks, so nobody watered the plants.
She also learned that the hot sun burned the leaves because there was no shade.
Her report must show each reason and what it caused.
She will add photos at the end.
evidence.stem: The answer was: a cause-and-effect chart. Tap 2 sentences that show a cause and its effect.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells the topic or the photos. Find the sentences that show what happened and why.

checks.passage: Topic: Litter in the school yard. The student will describe the problem and suggest three ways to fix it.
options: A list of dates and numbers
checks.why: The writing names a problem and solutions, so a problem-and-solution chart fits.

checks.passage: Topic: The life of a famous scientist, from birth to old age.
checks.why: Events across a whole life, in order of time, fit a timeline.

checks.passage: A student's web about "healthy habits" has five details for food and none for sleep.
checks.stem: What does the organizer show the student?
options: Food is not a healthy habit.
The sleep part needs more ideas.
The web should be thrown away.
checks.why: An empty part of the organizer shows where the topic needs more development.

again.title: What connection?
again.text:
Ask: **How are my ideas connected?**

By **time** → timeline. By **cause** → cause-and-effect chart. By **same and different** → Venn. By **problem and fix** → problem-solution chart.
again.example: "Why did the town flood?" Ideas are connected by **cause**. → **Cause-and-effect chart.**

slides.title: Prewriting strategies
slides.text:
Before drafting, writers use **prewriting strategies** to generate and shape ideas:

1. **Brainstorming:** listing every idea quickly.
2. **Freewriting:** writing nonstop to discover what you think.
3. **Questioning:** asking who, what, when, where, why, how.
4. **Outlining:** arranging main points and supporting details.
5. **Research notes and interviews:** gathering facts from sources and people.

slides.title: Strategy and purpose
slides.text:
The best strategy depends on the **purpose** and the **stage** of planning.

No topic yet? Brainstorm or freewrite. A topic but no facts? Ask research questions or interview someone. Ideas but no order? Outline.

slides.title: Planning an argument
slides.text:
For argument writing, an outline is powerful: claim, reasons in order of strength, evidence for each, and a counterclaim with a response.

It shows gaps before you begin, such as a reason without evidence.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To pick the best strategy, prove **where the writer is** in the process and **what the task demands**.

1. Find what the writer already has (a topic, facts, ideas, an order).
2. Find what is still missing.
3. Choose the strategy that supplies exactly that missing piece.

sentences.t: Laila must write a feature article about a local craftsman.
She has chosen her topic: an old man who makes traditional palm-leaf baskets.
She does not yet know how he learned the craft or what makes it special.
Her best next step is to interview him with prepared questions.

example.explain: Laila has a **topic** but lacks **information** that only the craftsman can give. An **interview** with prepared questions fills exactly that gap. Brainstorming would not supply those facts.

together.passage: Omar must write an argumentative essay on whether the city should ban cars from the old market streets. He has already read three articles and taken careful notes. His notes include facts about air quality, shop owners' opinions and the number of visitors each year. However, the notes are mixed together in the order he found them. He is not sure which reason is strongest or where the counterclaim should go. The essay is due on Thursday.
together.stem: Which prewriting strategy would help Omar most now?
options: Brainstorming a list of new topics
Making an outline that orders his claim, reasons, evidence and counterclaim
Interviewing a friend about his favourite food
together.hint: Omar already has a topic and facts. What is he missing?
together.good: Yes! His notes are complete but unordered, so an outline will arrange his reasons and place the counterclaim.

sentences: Omar must write an argumentative essay on whether the city should ban cars from the old market streets.
He has already read three articles and taken careful notes.
His notes include facts about air quality, shop owners' opinions and the number of visitors each year.
However, the notes are mixed together in the order he found them.
He is not sure which reason is strongest or where the counterclaim should go.
The essay is due on Thursday.
evidence.stem: The answer was an outline. Tap the 2 sentences that show what Omar still needs.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells the task, what he already has, or the due date. Find the sentences that show what is missing.

checks.passage: Noura must write a personal essay but has no idea what to write about.
options: Freewriting about memorable moments to discover a topic
checks.why: With no topic yet, freewriting helps her discover ideas.

checks.passage: Yousef is writing a report on how desert locusts swarm. He has a topic but almost no facts.
checks.stem: Which strategy should he use next?
options: Write research questions and look for answers in reliable sources
checks.why: He needs facts, so research questions guide what to look for.

checks.passage: A class is writing a persuasive letter about a new playground. They have many ideas but want to choose the best three reasons.
checks.stem: Which tool fits this step best?
options: A chart ranking each reason with its evidence
A Venn diagram of two playgrounds
checks.why: Ranking reasons with evidence helps them choose the strongest support for persuasion.

again.title: What is missing?
again.text:
Planning is like packing for a trip. Check what you **have** and what you **need**.

No idea → **brainstorm/freewrite**. No facts → **research/interview**. No order → **outline**.
again.example:
"I have lots of facts about camels, but they are all mixed up."

Missing: **order**. Strategy: **outline**.
